title: SaaS Metrics Dashboard Essentials: What Actually Goes On It
summary: See what belongs on a SaaS metrics dashboard: MRR, NRR, CAC, Rule of 40, burn multiple, and the data sources, tools, and cadence that keep boards informed.
body_markdown:
## What Goes on a SaaS Metrics Dashboard


A defensible SaaS metrics dashboard tracks roughly 18 metrics across five categories: revenue, retention, acquisition, efficiency, and cash. These are the same figures that recur across institutional SaaS benchmark surveys from SaaS Capital, KeyBanc, and Bessemer Venture Partners, the numbers investors, boards, and lenders already use to size up a company against its peers.


A dashboard like this isn’t just a screenshot for the board deck. It’s the shared source of truth every function points back to when the numbers disagree. A SaaS KPI dashboard template built around these five categories gives a controller, a VP of Finance, and a board member the same starting point, instead of three different spreadsheets telling three different stories.


Fewer metrics, more clarity.


Category Metric Formula Target band


Revenue MRR / ARR ARR = MRR x 12 Watch the trend, not just the level


Revenue Net New ARR New ARR + Expansion ARR minus Churned/Contraction ARR Growing quarter over quarter


Retention Gross Revenue Retention (GRR) (Starting Revenue minus Churn minus Contraction) / Starting Revenue Median around 88 percent (2024), per SaaS Capital


Retention Net Revenue Retention (NRR) GRR plus Expansion Revenue 118 percent enterprise, 108 percent mid-market, 97 percent SMB (SaaS Capital, 2025)


Acquisition LTV to CAC ratio LTV / CAC 3:1 or higher


Acquisition CAC Payback Period CAC / (ARPA x Gross Margin) ~18 months median, ~12 months top quartile (KeyBanc, 2025)


Acquisition Magic Number Change in ARR / prior quarter S&M spend 0.75 to 1.0+ signals the business is ready to scale spend


Efficiency Rule of 40 Revenue growth rate + profit margin 40 percent or higher


Efficiency Burn Multiple Net Burn / Net New ARR Under 1x excellent, 1x to 2x good, above 3x a serious problem


Cash Runway Cash Balance / Monthly Net Burn Tracked in months against the plan


Cash AR Days (DSO) (AR / Net Credit Sales) x Days in period Under 45 days generally healthy


### Revenue metrics


**Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR)** is the normalized monthly value of active subscription contracts. **Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR)** is simply MRR multiplied by 12, per[ChartMogul’s SaaS metrics glossary](https://chartmogul.com/saas-metrics/) , which is the core of the MRR ARR calculation most finance teams run every month.


MRR itself breaks into pieces that matter more than the headline number. **New MRR/ARR** is revenue from newly closed customers. **Expansion MRR/ARR** is additional revenue from existing customers, upsells, seat additions, cross-sells. **Churned/Contraction MRR** is revenue lost to cancellations and downgrades. **Net New ARR** nets those three together, New ARR plus Expansion ARR minus Churned and Contraction ARR, and it’s the denominator behind both the burn multiple and sales efficiency ratios below.


### Retention metrics


**Gross Revenue Retention (GRR)** measures the percentage of starting revenue kept after churn and downgrades, with expansion excluded, so it can never exceed 100 percent. GRR = (Starting Revenue minus Churn minus Contraction) divided by Starting Revenue, per[Maxio’s retention framework](https://www.maxio.com/saaspedia/gross-retention-vs-net-retention) . **Net Revenue Retention (NRR)** , sometimes called Net Dollar Retention, adds expansion revenue back in and can exceed 100 percent.


Median NRR splits sharply by segment: 118 percent for enterprise, 108 percent for mid-market, and 97 percent for SMB-focused companies, according to[SaaS Capital’s 2025 retention benchmarks](https://www.saas-capital.com/blog-posts/what-is-a-good-retention-rate-for-a-private-saas-company/) . The same report notes median NRR across the broader private SaaS market has drifted down from roughly 105 percent in 2021 to about 101 percent by 2024, a trend attributed to post-pandemic tool rationalization.


**Logo Retention Rate** counts retained accounts regardless of contract size, a different signal than revenue retention. A company can run high logo churn while posting strong NRR if the accounts leaving are small and the accounts staying expand, so a board dashboard should show both side by side rather than substitute one for the other. **Churn Rate** should always specify logo churn (accounts lost) or revenue churn (dollars lost), since the two frequently diverge in enterprise-weighted businesses.


### Acquisition metrics


**Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)** is fully loaded sales and marketing spend divided by new customers acquired in the period. **LTV** is Average Revenue Per Account multiplied by Gross Margin, divided by the churn rate, per[ChartMogul’s LTV formula](https://chartmogul.com/saas-metrics/ltv/) .


**LTV to CAC ratio.** The LTV CAC ratio calculation is simply LTV divided by CAC. A ratio of 3:1 or higher, LTV at least three times CAC, is the widely cited threshold for a capital-efficient SaaS business, a benchmark that shows up consistently across investor diligence checklists.


**CAC Payback Period** answers how many months it takes a new customer’s gross margin to repay their acquisition cost, CAC Payback = CAC / (ARPA x Gross Margin), per[Stripe’s explainer](https://stripe.com/resources/more/what-is-the-cac-payback-period) . Median payback fell to roughly 18 months in 2024, down from about 24 months the prior survey, with top-quartile companies near 12 months, according to the[KeyBanc Capital Markets 2025 SaaS Survey](https://seeto.ai/blog/keybanc-saas-survey-2025-takeaways) .


**Magic Number** measures sales efficiency with a one-quarter lag. Below 0.5 signals a go-to-market problem, 0.75 to 1.0 is the range where investors generally consider a company ready to scale spend, and growth investor IVP has cited its portfolio average at roughly 1.2, as reported by[SaaStr](https://www.saastr.com/ivp-the-average-saas-magic-number-is-1-2) . **Pipeline Coverage** , pipeline value divided by the revenue target, carries a traditional benchmark of 3x, though enterprise motions with lower win rates commonly need 4x to 7x, per[Clari’s pipeline coverage analysis](https://www.clari.com/blog/pipeline-coverage-best-practices/) .


### Efficiency metrics


**Rule of 40** states that revenue growth rate plus profit margin should equal or exceed 40 percent, per[Corporate Finance Institute](https://corporatefinanceinstitute.com/resources/valuation/rule-of-40) . Companies clearing that bar traded at roughly 1.7 times higher valuation multiples in Bessemer Venture Partners’ Cloud Index,[as covered by Fortune](https://fortune.com/2024/01/17/bessemer-venture-partners-rule-of-40-valuation-metric-changing) .


**Burn Multiple** , popularized by David Sacks of Craft Ventures, is Net Burn divided by Net New ARR, per[Sacks’ original writeup](https://sacks.substack.com/p/the-burn-multiple-51a7e43cb200) . Under 1x is excellent, 1x to 2x is good, and above 3x is a serious problem that calls for an immediate cost review.


Burn multiple below 1.5 is healthy.


**Sales Efficiency** is the same-period cousin of Magic Number, Net New ARR divided by same-period sales and marketing spend with no quarter lag, per[Scale Venture Partners’ primer](https://www.scalevp.com/blog/a-primer-on-saas-sales-efficiency) . **R&D as a percent of revenue** runs a median of 22 percent of ARR, rising to 24 percent for companies in the $3 million to $5 million ARR band, per[SaaS Capital’s 2026 spending benchmarks](https://www.saas-capital.com/blog-posts/spending-benchmarks-for-private-b2b-saas-companies/) .


### Cash metrics


**Cash** and **Net Burn** (cash revenue minus cash operating expenses) are the two inputs to **Runway** , Runway in months = Cash Balance / Monthly Net Burn. **AR Days** , also called Days Sales Outstanding, measures how long credit sales take to convert into cash, DSO = (Accounts Receivable / Net Credit Sales) x Number of Days, with under 45 days generally considered healthy, per[Corporate Finance Institute](https://corporatefinanceinstitute.com/resources/accounting/days-sales-outstanding/) . Rising DSO tightens working capital and shortens runway even when the P&L looks unchanged.


**Free Cash Flow (FCF)** is Operating Cash Flow minus Capital Expenditures, the cleanest single number for whether the business is actually generating or consuming cash. For the fuller runway and burn math behind this panel, see[what counts as an ideal burn rate for a growing company](https://www.indinero.com/blog/what-is-the-ideal-burn-rate-for-a-growing-company/) . For a shorter list built specifically for fundraising conversations, see[the SaaS metrics investors track most closely](https://www.indinero.com/blog/key-saas-metrics-for-investors/) .


## Data Sources + Integration


A SaaS metrics dashboard is only as trustworthy as the data pipeline feeding it, and that pipeline follows a fairly standard shape across growth-stage SaaS companies.


1. **Accounting platform** (QuickBooks Online or Oracle NetSuite) supplies GAAP-based financials, revenue recognized, COGS, operating expenses, cash balances, and the trial balance the whole dashboard ties back to. For a closer look at how these two platforms differ for a growing SaaS company, see[indinero’s NetSuite vs QuickBooks comparison](https://www.indinero.com/blog/netsuite-vs-quickbooks/) .
2. **Billing and subscription systems** (Stripe, Chargify) supply raw subscription events, new signups, upgrades, downgrades, and cancellations, before any aggregation happens.
3. **Subscription analytics platforms** (ChartMogul, Maxio) sit on top of the billing data and normalize it into cohort retention, churned MRR, expansion MRR, and the GRR/NRR figures boards ask for, per[Maxio’s SaaS metrics framework](https://www.maxio.com/saaspedia/gross-retention-vs-net-retention) .
4. **CRM systems** (Salesforce, HubSpot) supply the pipeline, opportunity, and win-rate data behind CAC, pipeline coverage, and Magic Number, since acquisition cost lives in the sales stack, not the accounting system.
5. **A BI layer** (Power BI, Tableau, Looker, or Google Looker Studio) blends the three sources above into one governed view, so a board member sees NRR next to burn multiple next to CAC payback on a single screen instead of three disconnected exports.


The failure mode is the same across all five layers. Someone exports a CSV from one system and pastes it into a spreadsheet feeding the dashboard. It breaks the moment a number changes upstream, and nobody remembers to update the paste.


Indinero’s approach to this pipeline is tool-neutral by design. The team integrates with your existing stack, including QuickBooks, Xero, NetSuite, Stripe, Brex, and Ramp, instead of requiring a proprietary platform, so the data stays portable and the dashboard reflects the books rather than a parallel shadow ledger built from raw exports.


## Tool Choices


Growth-stage SaaS teams typically pick between general BI platforms and purpose-built subscription analytics tools, and the right choice depends on the existing stack.


Tool Pricing (checked 2026) Best fit


Microsoft Power BI Free individual tier. Pro $14/user/month, Premium Per User $24/user/month, both billed yearly, per[Microsoft’s pricing page](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/products/power-bi/pricing) Teams already on Microsoft 365 wanting affordable, governed reporting


Tableau Cloud Standard: Viewer $15, Explorer $42, Creator $75/user/month, billed annually, per[Tableau’s pricing page](https://www.tableau.com/pricing) Teams that need rich visual exploration and a dedicated analytics function


Google Looker Studio Free tier for Google-native sources. Looker Studio Pro is $9/user/project/month Lean, early-stage teams on a Google-centric stack without a BI budget


Looker (Google Cloud) No public pricing. Enterprise deployments commonly run $50,000 to $150,000+/year Larger organizations wanting one governed semantic layer feeding many BI consumers


ChartMogul Free up to $120K ARR. Starter $59 to $499/month, Pro $99 to $1,199/month, per[ChartMogul’s pricing page](https://chartmogul.com/pricing/) Subscription businesses wanting MRR/ARR/churn analytics live within days


Maxio Grow plan $599/month for up to $100K in monthly billings, per[Maxio’s pricing page](https://www.maxio.com/pricing) Companies wanting usage-based billing, revenue recognition, and SaaS metrics in one system


- **Power BI** fits teams already on Microsoft 365 or Excel who want DAX-based modeling without a big new line item.
- **Tableau** fits teams that need the richest visual exploration and can dedicate an analyst to manage licensing and cost as usage scales.
- **Google Looker Studio** is the cheapest entry point, free for Google-native sources, though third-party connectors typically add $20 to $350 or more per month.
- **Looker** fits larger organizations that have outgrown ad hoc dashboards and have the data engineering resources to build a certified semantic layer once and reuse it everywhere.
- **ChartMogul and Maxio** are purpose-built for subscription metrics. They get to MRR, ARR, and NRR faster than a general BI tool, but neither replaces a full reporting layer for the rest of the P&L.


Power BI and Tableau are general-purpose BI tools. They need financial, billing, and CRM data piped in before they show anything SaaS-specific, the same integration work that comes up across[cloud-based accounting platforms](https://www.indinero.com/blog/cloud-based-accounting-platforms/) generally. ChartMogul and Maxio start from the opposite direction, purpose-built for subscription data and quick to MRR, ARR, and NRR, but they won’t replace a general reporting layer for non-subscription data.


## Board Reporting Cadence


Growth-stage SaaS finance teams typically run a four-layer reporting cadence, from a weekly operating review to an annual operating plan.


That structure runs a weekly operating review for the leadership team, a monthly business review tied to the close, a quarterly board deck, and an annual operating plan that resets targets, per[CrunchSpark’s board reporting guide](https://crunchspark.com/board-reporting-growth-companies.html) . Each layer moves slower and covers fewer, more strategic metrics than the one below it.


A board deck typically opens with five to seven headline metrics: current ARR/MRR and growth rate, NRR, net new ARR/MRR by month, CAC and CAC payback period, and burn rate with runway in months. These same numbers double as the CFO dashboard KPIs a board expects to see in the deck every quarter. The supporting KPI dashboard behind that summary carries 8 to 12 metrics, trended over at least six months and shown against target, per the same source and[Fairview’s executive reporting framework](https://getfairview.com/executive-reporting) .


Variance commentary is what separates a usable board pack from a data dump. Every material variance needs a sentence or two explaining what happened and why, not just a red number.


A number without a reason is unfinished work.


Many finance teams color-code variance thresholds, flagging deviations around 5 percent yellow and 10 percent red, with a notes column so department heads don’t have to schedule a separate meeting to explain a miss. Month-to-month SaaS metrics are noisy, since a single large contract renewal or cancellation can swing MRR growth for one month, while quarter-over-quarter comparisons smooth that noise out and better reflect the trend a board is actually trying to evaluate.

## Common Dashboard Mistakes


The most common SaaS dashboard mistakes share one root cause: metrics get added faster than anyone prunes them.


1.


**Vanity metrics crowding out decision metrics.** Total signups, page views, downloads, and social followers look impressive but don’t change what a finance or leadership team decides to do next, a pattern documented in[Baremetrics’ rundown of common SaaS vanity metrics](https://baremetrics.com/blog/7-common-vanity-metrics-that-youve-been-using) . Mixing them onto the same dashboard as MRR and CAC just dilutes the metrics that actually matter. The fix is simple: keep vanity metrics off the board deck entirely.


2.


**Too many metrics with no hierarchy.** Dashboards that track 30 or 40 metrics with no prioritization create noise, not clarity, MRR sitting next to Instagram followers, CAC sitting next to blog traffic. The fix is a hard cap of 5 to 7 headline metrics for an executive view and 8 to 12 for the supporting KPI layer, each one tied to a specific decision.


3.


**Lagging-only metrics with no leading indicators.** A dashboard built entirely from trailing GAAP numbers tells a board what already happened but gives no early warning. Pairing lagging metrics like NRR with leading ones like pipeline coverage, Magic Number, and CAC payback trend gives a board something it can act on before the next close.


4.


**No connection to action.** Before a metric earns a permanent spot on the dashboard, it should pass a simple test: what decision would the team make differently based on a change in this number? If the answer is unclear, the metric belongs in a supporting report, not the executive view.[Indinero’s SaaS financial decision tree](https://www.indinero.com/resources/saas-financial-decision-tree/) walks through that same kind of test for the metrics that matter most at each funding stage.


5.


**Manual entry instead of automated integration.** Dashboards fed by someone exporting a CSV from the billing system and pasting it into a spreadsheet break the moment an upstream number changes, and nobody remembers to refresh the paste. Automated integration from the accounting platform, billing system, and CRM into the BI layer keeps every number current and removes the version-control risk of hand-maintained spreadsheets.

## Frequently asked questions


Still deciding what belongs on your SaaS metrics dashboard and where the numbers should come from? These are the questions finance leads ask most before they build one.


### What metrics actually belong on a SaaS dashboard?


A SaaS metrics dashboard should track about 18 metrics across five categories: revenue, retention, acquisition, efficiency, and cash. Signup counts, page views, and social followers don’t belong there since they don’t change what a finance team decides to do next. Indinero builds these dashboards as part of fractional CFO advisory, tying each metric to a specific category instead of a scattershot list pulled from three disconnected spreadsheets.


### How are MRR and ARR calculated and which one should the board see?


Monthly Recurring Revenue is the normalized monthly value of active subscription contracts, and Annual Recurring Revenue is simply MRR multiplied by 12. Boards typically see ARR as the headline figure since it standardizes revenue for scale and comparison, while MRR feeds the month-to-month trend line underneath it. Indinero’s board reporting cadence tracks both, alongside net new ARR and NRR, because a single snapshot without the trend hides whether growth is accelerating or stalling.


### What is the right way to calculate LTV/CAC ratio?


The LTV to CAC ratio is calculated by dividing customer lifetime value by customer acquisition cost, with 3 to 1 or higher considered capital efficient. LTV equals average revenue per account times gross margin, divided by the churn rate, while CAC is fully loaded sales and marketing spend divided by new customers acquired in the period. Indinero calculates both from the same reconciled GAAP financials behind the monthly close, so the ratio reflects actual margin and spend rather than a rough estimate pulled from a spreadsheet.


### What data sources need to feed the dashboard?


A SaaS metrics dashboard needs data from five sources: the accounting platform, billing system, subscription analytics tool, CRM, and BI layer. QuickBooks or NetSuite supplies GAAP-based financials, Stripe or Chargify feed raw subscription events, and ChartMogul or Maxio normalize those into churn and retention figures. Indinero integrates directly with a client’s existing stack, including QuickBooks, NetSuite, and Stripe, instead of requiring a proprietary platform, so the dashboard reflects the books rather than a set of manual exports.


### What tools do most growing SaaS companies use for dashboards?


Growing SaaS companies typically choose between general BI platforms like Power BI and Tableau and purpose-built tools like ChartMogul and Maxio for subscription metrics. The right pick depends on the existing stack, since teams already on Microsoft 365 often default to Power BI while ChartMogul and Maxio get to MRR, ARR, and NRR faster than a general BI tool. Indinero connects whichever BI tool a client already uses to their accounting, billing, and CRM data instead of requiring a single proprietary platform.


### What is the right cadence for board reporting?


Board reporting typically follows four layers: weekly operating reviews, a monthly business review, a quarterly board deck, and an annual operating plan. Each layer moves slower and covers fewer, more strategic metrics than the one below it, with a board deck typically opening on five to seven headline numbers like ARR, NRR, and burn rate with runway. Indinero builds this cadence into its fractional CFO advisory, pairing every material variance with a sentence explaining what happened rather than leaving the board to guess at a red number.


### What are the most common dashboard mistakes?


The most common SaaS dashboard mistakes are vanity metrics crowding out decision metrics and too many numbers with no hierarchy. Other errors include tracking only lagging GAAP numbers with no leading indicators, keeping metrics that don’t tie to a decision, and feeding the dashboard from manually pasted spreadsheet exports that break when an upstream number changes. Indinero avoids that last failure point by connecting the accounting platform, billing system, and CRM directly into the BI layer, so every number stays current without anyone remembering to refresh a paste.
